event-001.summary: Battle in 490 BC in which the army of Athens defeated a Persian landing force on a plain by the sea.
facts: The first marathon race, held in 1896, was inspired by the legend of a messenger who ran to Athens with news of the victory.
Herodotus wrote that 6,400 Persians and 192 Athenians were killed.

event-002.summary: Campaign begun in 334 BC in which the young king of Macedonia toppled Persia and pushed on to the threshold of India.
facts: He founded several cities named Alexandria, and the one in Egypt survives to this day.
Hellenism, a blend of Greek and Eastern cultures, emerged from it.

event-003.summary: Starting in 264 BC, three wars over nearly 120 years in which Rome and Carthage fought for control of the Mediterranean.
facts: In 218 BC, Hannibal led 37 elephants across the Alps.
In 146 BC, Carthage was burned to the ground and Rome took control of the Mediterranean.

event-004.summary: In 476, the Germanic mercenary leader Odoacer deposed the last emperor, a mere boy.
facts: This year is often taken as the end of Antiquity and the start of the European Middle Ages.
Rome's eastern half held out for nearly another thousand years before falling in 1453.

event-005.summary: A religion that began around 610 with revelations received by Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, and went on to unite Arabia.
facts: The year 622, when he moved from Mecca to Medina, is year one of its calendar.
Within a century it had spread across North Africa and into the Iberian Peninsula.

event-006.summary: Beginning in 1096 and lasting nearly 200 years, a series of campaigns in which European knights invaded the Middle East to retake the Holy Land.
facts: They captured Jerusalem in 1099 but lost it to Saladin in 1187.
They opened a channel through which goods and knowledge from the East flowed into Europe.

event-007.summary: A document that English barons forced King John to accept in 1215, stating that even the king must obey the law.
facts: Three of its clauses are still law in England and Wales today.
Four original copies survive: two at the British Library and one each at Lincoln Castle and Salisbury Cathedral.

event-008.summary: In the 13th century, Genghis Khan and his descendants swept on horseback from China to Eastern Europe.
facts: After Genghis Khan rose to power in 1206, the empire reached its greatest extent under his grandson Kublai.
At its peak it covered 23.5 million square kilometers, the largest contiguous empire in history.

event-009.summary: An epidemic that arrived in 1347 on ships from the Black Sea and killed more than a third of Europe's population.
facts: The English word “quarantine” comes from the Venetian term for holding ships in isolation for 40 days.
With workers suddenly scarce, serfdom began to crumble.

event-010.summary: From 1337, an on-and-off conflict lasting 116 years in which England and France fought over the throne and territory.
facts: In 1429, Joan of Arc lifted the siege of Orléans and turned the tide of the war.
When the war ended, England had lost all its lands on the Continent except Calais.

event-011.summary: From the 14th century, a cultural movement in which Italian cities revived the ideals of ancient Greece and Rome and placed humanity at the center.
facts: The Medici, a banking family of Florence, became leading patrons of artists.
It reached its height around 1500 with Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo.

event-012.summary: Around 1450, a goldsmith in Mainz began casting letters in metal so that books could be mass-produced.
facts: Its best-known work is the 42-line Bible, printed around 1455.
Korea's “Jikji,” printed under the Goryeo dynasty, predates it by more than 70 years.

event-013.summary: In 1453, Ottoman forces breached the walls with giant cannons and seized the thousand-year-old capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.
facts: The walls were breached on May 29 after a 53-day siege.
The city is today's Istanbul, the largest city in Turkey.

event-014.summary: In 1492, a captain trying to reach India by sailing west landed instead on an island in the Caribbean.
facts: Because he believed he had reached India, the Caribbean islands are still called the West Indies.
Afterward potatoes, corn, and chili peppers spread across the ocean, while smallpox crossed over to the Americas.

event-015.summary: In 1517, a movement that split the Church in two after the German monk Martin Luther challenged the sale of indulgences.
facts: Luther is said to have posted his theses on the door of a church in Wittenberg.
October 31, the day he supposedly posted them, is still a public holiday in nine German states.

event-016.summary: Setting out in 1519, a Spanish fleet named the Pacific for its calm waters and became the first to sail all the way around the Earth.
facts: About 270 men left on five ships; only one ship and 18 men made it back.
The captain himself was killed in the Philippines and never saw the voyage's end.

event-017.summary: In 1588, Spain sent nearly 130 ships to invade England but was beaten in the Strait of Dover.
facts: Anchored off Calais, the fleet was scattered by English fireships.
On the way home, storms off Scotland and Ireland sank more ships than the fighting had.

event-018.summary: A war that began in 1618 as a clash between Protestants and Catholics and drew in most of Europe.
facts: In parts of Germany, where most of the fighting took place, the population fell by more than half.
The spark was the defenestration of Prague, when imperial officials were thrown out of a window at Prague Castle.

event-019.summary: The 1648 agreement that ended the Thirty Years' War and set the principle that states should not meddle in one another's internal affairs.
facts: It was signed in two cities, Münster and Osnabrück.
Switzerland won legal recognition of its independence from the Holy Roman Empire.

event-020.summary: In 1688, a nearly bloodless coup in which the English Parliament replaced the king.
facts: James II fled, and his daughter Mary and her husband William took the throne together.
The next year, the Bill of Rights barred the Crown from levying taxes without Parliament's consent.

event-021.summary: From the late 18th century, a transformation that began in Britain as steam engines and factories replaced human hands and changed everyday life entirely.
facts: It began in cotton mills that brought in spinning machines.
The watt (W) printed on light bulbs is named after James Watt, who improved the steam engine.

event-022.summary: The 1776 document in which thirteen colonies announced to the world that they were breaking away from Great Britain.
facts: July 4, the day it was adopted, is now Independence Day in the United States.
Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft, which includes the words “all men are created equal.”

event-023.summary: In 1789, the people of Paris rose up, toppled the old class system, and claimed sovereignty for the nation.
facts: It began with the storming of the Bastille on July 14, now France's national holiday.
France's motto, “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity,” was first raised at this time.

event-024.summary: In 1814, after Napoleon's fall, representatives of Europe's monarchies met to redraw the continent's borders.
facts: Austrian Chancellor Metternich steered it toward restoring the pre-revolutionary order.
Amid an endless round of balls, the talks dragged on for nine months, earning the nickname “the dancing congress.”

event-025.summary: In 1839, the United Kingdom went to war after Qing China seized and destroyed drugs belonging to British merchants.
facts: Under the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, the defeated Qing ceded Hong Kong Island.
Hong Kong remained British for more than 150 years before returning to China in 1997.

event-026.summary: Beginning in 1861, a four-year war fought after Southern states seceded to defend slavery and the North fought back.
facts: In 1863, in the middle of the war, Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation.
More than 620,000 people died, still the highest death toll of any war in the history of the United States.

event-027.summary: Sparked in 1914 by the assassination of an heir to the throne in Sarajevo, a four-year conflict of trenches and machine guns.
facts: November 11, the day of the 1918 armistice, is a national holiday in France and a day of remembrance in the United Kingdom.
Four empires collapsed in its wake: the German, Austrian, Russian, and Ottoman.

event-028.summary: In 1917, an uprising in which workers and soldiers overthrew the tsar and set up the world's first socialist government.
facts: The February Revolution forced the tsar to step down, and in the October Revolution Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power.
When the country switched calendars the next year, the anniversary of the October Revolution moved to November 7.

event-029.summary: An economic slump that began with the 1929 stock market crash in New York City and spread around the world for nearly a decade.
facts: The trigger was the crash of October 24, known as “Black Thursday.”
With unemployment in the United States approaching 25 percent, the New Deal put people to work building dams and roads.

event-030.summary: Beginning in 1939 with Germany's invasion of Poland, a six-year conflict that engulfed every continent.
facts: More than 60 million people died, making it the deadliest war in history.
Japan surrendered after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

event-031.summary: In 1969, American astronauts became the first humans to set foot on another world.
facts: After touching down on July 20, Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the lunar surface for about two and a half hours.
Some 600 million people around the world watched it live on television.

event-032.summary: On November 9, 1989, the barrier dividing East Germany and West Germany was torn down by ordinary citizens.
facts: It was set off when an East German spokesman mistakenly told a press conference that the border would open “immediately.”
East and West reunited the following October 3, now Germany's national holiday.

event-033.summary: Around 3500 BC, the Sumerians of the plain between two rivers built the first cities and invented cuneiform writing.
facts: They pressed letters into clay tablets with reed pens.
The base-60 system that divides an hour into 60 minutes and a circle into 360 degrees came from here.

event-034.summary: Beginning around 3000 BC, a civilization along the Nile that relied on the river's yearly floods and endured for 3,000 years.
facts: At 146 meters, the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest structure on Earth for more than 3,700 years.
Its calendar had 365 days: twelve 30-day months plus five extra days.

event-035.summary: Around 2500 BC, a civilization in a great river basin with cities laid out in neat grids and equipped with sewers.
facts: Its leading city, Mohenjo-daro, still has a 12-meter-long brick bath known as the Great Bath.
Thousands of inscriptions have been found on seals and other objects, but no one has yet deciphered them.

event-036.summary: Around 2000 BC, East Asia's first civilization arose along a muddy, silt-laden river, leaving behind bronzes and oracle bone script.
facts: Divination records carved on turtle shells became the roots of Chinese characters.
Excavation of Yinxu, the last capital of the Shang dynasty, began in 1928.

event-037.summary: Around 1750 BC, a king of Babylon carved laws such as “an eye for an eye” onto a stone pillar.
facts: Blinding a noble cost you your own eye, but blinding a commoner could be settled with a payment of silver.
The 2.25-meter stone pillar covered in its laws is now in the Louvre in Paris.

event-038.summary: Around the 6th century BC, the teachings of Siddhartha, who gave up his life as a prince and attained enlightenment.
facts: Buddha's Birthday, on the 8th day of the 4th lunar month, is a public holiday in South Korea.
He is said to have attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.

event-039.summary: In 221 BC, a king from the western frontier conquered six rival states and became the first ruler to call himself emperor.
facts: He standardized writing, weights and measures, and even the width of cart axles.
By linking up the northern defensive walls, he laid the foundation for the Great Wall of China.

event-040.summary: An east–west trade route opened in the 2nd century BC when Emperor Wu of Han sent envoys to the Western Regions.
facts: The envoy Zhang Qian returned after 13 years and reported on the lands to the west.
The name was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.

event-041.summary: From the late 6th century, a system under which the Sui dynasty began choosing officials by competitive tests rather than family background.
facts: It lasted more than 1,300 years until it was abolished in 1905, near the end of the Qing dynasty.
Korea's Goryeo dynasty adopted the system in 958 under King Gwangjong.

event-042.summary: From 1405, seven voyages in which a great Ming fleet sailed through Southeast Asia as far as the east coast of Africa.
facts: The first voyage set out with 317 ships and nearly 28,000 men, almost 90 years before Christopher Columbus.
The voyages stopped after a new emperor took the throne, and the court is said to have deliberately destroyed the records.

event-043.summary: Beginning in 1592 with Japan's invasion of Joseon, a seven-year war that drew in Joseon, Ming China, and Japan.
facts: Off Hansan Island, Yi Sun-sin's navy crushed the Japanese fleet using the crane-wing formation.
The face on the front of South Korea's 100-won coin is Yi Sun-sin, who led the navy in this war.

event-044.summary: In 1868, a reform in which Japan swept away the shogunate and adopted Western-style institutions under the emperor.
facts: It abolished the class system and introduced military conscription and compulsory education.
In 1872, Japan's first railway opened between Shimbashi in Tokyo and Yokohama.

event-045.summary: In 1911, an uprising by soldiers in Wuchang that ended more than 2,000 years of imperial rule.
facts: October 10, the day of the uprising, is now Taiwan's national day, and the Republic of China was founded the following January.
In 1912, six-year-old Puyi, the last emperor, gave up the throne.

event-046.summary: In the 3rd century BC, a Maurya king, horrified by the carnage of his conquest of Kalinga, repented and spread the teachings far and wide.
facts: The four lions carved on one of his stone pillars became the model for India's national emblem.
He sent envoys to carry the teachings as far as Sri Lanka.

event-047.summary: From the 4th century, an era when a dynasty that united northern India saw the number zero and classical Sanskrit culture flourish.
facts: The digits 0 through 9 used today originated here and traveled to Europe by way of the Arab world.
Hinduism took on its present form during this period.

event-048.summary: A state that rose around 1299 from a small Turkic tribe in Anatolia and lasted more than 600 years.
facts: Named after its founder, Osman I, it endured until 1922.
It governed by recognizing each religious group as its own community.

event-049.summary: In 1526, Babur, who came down from Central Asia, founded a state in northern India that blended Islamic and Hindu cultures.
facts: The Taj Mahal is the tomb that Shah Jahan spent more than 20 years building in memory of his late wife.
Emperor Akbar abolished the tax levied on non-Muslims.

event-050.summary: In 1532, a great Andean empire fell to an expedition of just 168 men led by Pizarro.
facts: Guns and horses mattered, but more decisive was smallpox, which spread ahead of the invaders, killed the emperor, and sparked a civil war.
Instead of writing, it recorded numbers on knotted cords called quipu.

event-051.summary: From the 16th to the 19th century, the trade in which European merchants sold Africans to plantations in the Americas.
facts: It formed one leg of the triangular trade linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas.
An estimated 12 million or more people were carried off on slave ships.

event-052.summary: In 1857, an uprising launched by Indian soldiers of the British East India Company that spread across northern India.
facts: It was ignited by rumors that cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat.
The year after it was crushed, the East India Company lost its power to govern, and the British Crown took direct rule of India.

event-053.summary: In 1884, a meeting at which the European powers gathered to set rules for carving up an entire continent.
facts: Not a single person from the lands being divided was invited.
By 1914, Ethiopia and Liberia were the only independent countries left in Africa.

event-054.summary: In 1904, a war between two countries over control of Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula.
facts: At the Battle of Tsushima in 1905, Russia's Baltic Fleet was almost entirely destroyed.
That same year, Japan used the Eulsa Treaty to strip the Korean Empire of its diplomatic rights.

event-055.summary: During World War II, Nazi Germany's systematic murder of Jews and other minorities.
facts: About 6 million Jews alone are estimated to have been killed.
January 27, the day Auschwitz was liberated, is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

event-056.summary: An organization created in 1945 by countries that had lived through two world wars, to keep the peace together.
facts: Its charter was adopted in San Francisco, and it came into being on October 24, now celebrated as United Nations Day.
The five permanent members of the Security Council hold veto power.

event-057.summary: In 1947, after nonviolent resistance led by Mahatma Gandhi, the country broke free of nearly 200 years of British rule.
facts: In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi led the Salt March, a 24-day walk to the sea.
Independence on August 15 split the land into India and Pakistan, and it falls on the same date as South Korea's Liberation Day.

event-058.summary: Begun in 1950 by North Korea's invasion of the South, the Cold War's first hot war, to which 16 UN member states sent combat troops.
facts: The guns fell silent on July 27, 1953, when the armistice was signed at Panmunjom.
Because it ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty, the Military Demarcation Line remains to this day.

event-059.summary: Thirteen days in October 1962 when the United States and the Soviet Union came to the brink of war over Soviet nuclear weapons on a Caribbean island.
facts: The Soviet Union withdrew its missiles, and the United States secretly agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey.
Afterward, a direct hotline was set up between the two countries' leaders.

event-060.summary: In 1994, the laws that separated people by skin color collapsed, and people of all races voted together for the first time.
facts: That election made Nelson Mandela, who had spent 27 years in prison, president.
A Truth and Reconciliation Commission was set up to confront the past.

event-061.summary: In 1991, a socialist federation that had lasted nearly 70 years broke apart into fifteen countries.
facts: On December 25, the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin and Gorbachev stepped down.
Russia took over its permanent seat on the UN Security Council.

event-062.summary: From 508 BC, a system in which citizens gathered in an assembly to decide public affairs and public offices were filled by lot.
facts: Cleisthenes reorganized the tribes by place of residence instead of by kinship.
Later, selection by lot and pay for public service let even poor citizens hold office.

event-063.summary: In 480 BC, a sea battle in which the allied Greek fleet lured the Persian fleet into a narrow strait and turned the tide of the war.
facts: Themistocles tricked the enemy into a strait too tight for their large ships to maneuver.
The victory put an end to Persia's attempt to conquer Greece.

event-064.summary: Starting in 431 BC, a 27-year war within Greece in which Athens and Sparta fought for supremacy.
facts: A plague swept through Athens and killed its leader, Pericles.
Thucydides' account of the war became a model for historical writing.

event-065.summary: In 550 BC, Cyrus the Great united the ancient Near East and let conquered peoples keep their own faiths, launching a new empire.
facts: In 539 BC he entered Babylon and allowed the captive Jews to return home.
The “Neither snow nor rain…” inscription on a New York City post office describes this empire's mounted couriers.

event-066.summary: In 509 BC, a city on the Tiber drove out its king and began electing two men each year to run the state.
facts: Two consuls split power equally so that each could check the other.
SPQR, stamped even on manhole covers in Rome, stands for “the Senate and People of Rome.”

event-067.summary: In 27 BC, Octavian, who had ended the civil wars, received the title “the revered one” and became the first emperor in all but name.
facts: That title, Augustus, survives in the English name of the month August.
It was followed by roughly 200 years of relative peace.

event-068.summary: The dynasty founded in 202 BC by Liu Bang, a man of peasant origins, after the fall of the Qin.
facts: He defeated Xiang Yu of Chu to become emperor; these are the same Han and Chu that face off in janggi, Korean chess.
Its name lives on in the term “Han Chinese” and in “hanzi,” the Chinese word for Chinese characters.

event-069.summary: Around the 11th century BC, the Phoenicians boiled picture writing down into 22 symbols for sounds.
facts: Its first two letters, aleph (ox) and bet (house), became the Greek alpha and beta, which gave the alphabet its name.
By way of Greece and Rome, it became the root of the scripts used in Europe today.

event-070.summary: From around 2000 BC, a civilization that built stepped pyramids in the jungles of Central America and understood the concept of zero.
facts: Its kings' histories were recorded in hieroglyphs carved in stone.
Its precise calendars tracked the movements of the Sun and Venus.

event-071.summary: In 776 BC, the Greeks began holding a festival of athletic contests in honor of Zeus every four years.
facts: For the first 50 years or so, the only event was a single footrace of less than 200 meters.
The first modern Olympics, held in Athens in 1896, revived the name.

event-072.summary: In 313, Emperor Constantine issued a decision in Milan granting legal tolerance to a persecuted religion.
facts: In 321, he ordered city officials and residents to rest and workshops to close on Sundays.
In 380, under Emperor Theodosius, it became the state religion of the empire.

event-073.summary: Beginning in 376, northern tribes driven by the Huns poured across Rome's frontiers and redrew the map of Europe.
facts: The Visigoths crossed the Danube, and in 410 they sacked Rome.
The word “vandalism” comes from the Vandals, who also sacked Rome.

event-074.summary: The dynasty founded in 618 after the fall of the Sui, with its capital at Chang'an, that became the center of East Asia.
facts: People from Persia and Silla lived side by side in Chang'an.
Li Bai and Du Fu wrote their poetry under this dynasty.

event-075.summary: An Islamic state that rose in 750 by overthrowing the Umayyads and gathered scholars in its round capital, Baghdad.
facts: At the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, Greek texts were translated into Arabic.
The word “algorithm” comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a scholar at the House of Wisdom.

event-076.summary: In 751, Tang and Abbasid armies clashed by a river in Central Asia, and the Tang suffered a crushing defeat.
facts: The Tang army was led by Go Seonji, a general descended from refugees of Goguryeo.
Legend has it that captured Tang craftsmen passed on the secret of papermaking.

event-077.summary: In 800, the Pope placed a crown on the head of the Frankish king, and a new empire arose in Western Europe.
facts: He was crowned during Christmas Mass at St. Peter's Basilica in Rome.
Today's France, Germany, and Italy all emerged from his lands.

event-078.summary: From 793, seafarers from the northern seas sailed up rivers and raided their way across Europe.
facts: The name Bluetooth comes from the nickname of Harald, the 10th-century Viking king who united Denmark.
They didn't just raid; they also settled in places like Novgorod and Normandy.

event-079.summary: In 755, an eight-year revolt launched by a frontier military governor that sent the Tang into decline.
facts: Led by An Lushan and Shi Siming, it captured both capitals, Luoyang and Chang'an.
Afterward, the Tang never regained control over regional powers.

event-080.summary: In 1066, a duke who crossed from northern France won at Hastings, and the island changed hands.
facts: On Christmas Day that year, Duke William was crowned king at Westminster Abbey.
Even “beef” and “pork” come from the French spoken by the Norman nobility.

event-081.summary: In 1054, the Pope in Rome and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, and the two churches went their separate ways.
facts: The two churches still calculate Easter differently, so in many years they celebrate it on different dates.
The split lives on today in the Catholic and Orthodox churches.

event-082.summary: Two creations of Tang and Song China: a powder discovered while searching for an elixir of immortality, and a needle that points south.
facts: In 1044, the Song military manual “Wujing Zongyao” became the first text to record a formula for gunpowder.
In late Goryeo, Choe Mu-seon made gunpowder and cannons and used them to burn Japanese pirate ships at Jinpo.

event-083.summary: For nearly 800 years until 1492, the Christian kingdoms of Iberia fought to win back land from Muslim rulers.
facts: It ended with the fall of Granada, the last Muslim kingdom, whose palace is the Alhambra.
That same year, the Spanish crown backed Christopher Columbus's voyage.

event-084.summary: The 12th century, when the kings of ancient Cambodia built huge temples and waterways deep in the jungle and dominated Southeast Asia.
facts: Angkor Wat was built under Suryavarman II.
Angkor Wat appears in the center of the flag of Cambodia.

event-085.summary: From the 13th century, an alliance of merchant cities on the Baltic and North Seas that jointly controlled shipping routes and prices.
facts: Centered on Lübeck, it once brought together nearly 200 cities.
Hamburg and Bremen still include “Free Hanseatic City” in their official names.

event-086.summary: Around 1325, the Mexica founded their capital on an island in the middle of a lake and went on to rule central Mexico.
facts: Today's Mexico City stands on the site of their capital, Tenochtitlan.
The eagle perched on a cactus on Mexico's flag comes from the legend of the city's founding.

event-087.summary: The dynasty founded in 1368 by Zhu Yuanzhang, a former wandering monk, after he drove the Mongols back north.
facts: The Forbidden City in Beijing was completed under this dynasty in 1420.
Most of the Great Wall of China that survives today was built under this dynasty.

event-088.summary: In 1498, a Portuguese fleet rounded the southern tip of Africa and became the first to reach the pepper-rich waters of Asia by that route.
facts: Ten months after leaving Lisbon, it arrived at Calicut on India's southwest coast.
The pepper and cinnamon it brought back paid for the voyage dozens of times over.

event-089.summary: In 1494, Spain and Portugal moved a line drawn by the Pope farther west and split the newly discovered world between them.
facts: The line was drawn 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands.
This line is why Brazil is the only country in South America where Portuguese is spoken.

event-090.summary: In 1521, Cortés's Spanish expedition, aided by smallpox, destroyed a capital built on a lake.
facts: The words “tomato” and “avocado” come from Nahuatl, the language its people spoke.
Neighboring peoples who bore grudges against them sided with the Spanish.

event-091.summary: In 1603, Ieyasu set up in a small castle beside a marsh and founded a samurai government that lasted more than 260 years.
facts: Edo, the Tokugawa family's base, is today's Tokyo.
Daimyo were required to live in Edo every other year, which drained their power.

event-092.summary: In 1644, a power that rose in Manchuria crossed Shanhai Pass and entered Beijing, founding China's last imperial dynasty.
facts: The qipao is generally believed to have evolved from the dress of Manchu women, the people who founded this dynasty.
In 1636 it invaded Korea's Joseon kingdom, and the following year King Injo surrendered at Samjeondo.

event-093.summary: In the 17th century, a shift in which thinkers like Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton began studying nature through observation and experiment rather than old books.
facts: Telescopes and microscopes opened up worlds invisible to the naked eye.
In 1687, Isaac Newton's “Principia” explained the motions of the heavens and the Earth with one set of laws.

event-094.summary: In the 18th century, a movement in which French thinkers called on human reason to challenge outdated authority.
facts: Voltaire, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and Montesquieu were at its heart.
The separation of powers that Montesquieu set out in “The Spirit of the Laws” in 1748 was written into the U.S. Constitution.

event-095.summary: Beginning in 1756, a global conflict that grew out of a dispute in North America and spread to Europe and India.
facts: Britain defeated France and took control of North America and India.
Its attempt to pay off war debts by taxing the colonies helped spark American independence.

event-096.summary: Starting in 1697, a Russian tsar who toured Western Europe incognito came home and overhauled his entire country.
facts: To learn shipbuilding, he worked with his own hands in a Dutch shipyard.
In 1703, he founded a new capital, Saint Petersburg, on marshland.

event-097.summary: From 1803, twelve years of war in which the French emperor's armies swept across most of Europe before being driven back.
facts: Of the more than 450,000 men who set out on the 1812 invasion of Russia, only about 120,000 survived.
After his first abdication, the Congress of Vienna met to redraw Europe's borders.

event-098.summary: From the 1810s, a wave in which the colonies of Spain and Portugal broke away one after another to form their own nations.
facts: Bolivia is named after Simón Bolívar.
Only in Brazil did a prince declare independence himself, so less blood was shed.

event-099.summary: In the 19th century, a nearly century-long trend in which country after country outlawed the buying and selling of human beings.
facts: The United Kingdom banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833.
After its civil war, the United States abolished slavery in 1865 with the 13th Amendment.

event-100.summary: In 1861, a peninsula long divided into many states became a single kingdom under the King of Sardinia.
facts: Giuseppe Garibaldi and his Redshirts swept up from the south.
Rome was the last to join, in 1870.

event-101.summary: In 1871, scattered states were bound together into a single empire under Prussian leadership.
facts: It was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, in a France that had just been defeated.
Defeated France gave up Alsace-Lorraine, and the resentment lingered all the way to World War I.

event-102.summary: In 1853, an American fleet led by its “black ships” arrived to demand that Japan open its doors.
facts: It appeared in Edo Bay and secured the Convention of Kanagawa the following year.
The shock shook the shogunate and led to the Meiji Restoration.

event-103.summary: Beginning in late 1850, a 14-year uprising led by Hong Xiuquan, who had failed the civil service exams again and again, under the banner of a new faith.
facts: Calling himself the younger brother of Jesus, he captured Nanjing and made it his capital.
More than 20 million people are estimated to have died.

event-104.summary: Opened in 1869, a waterway linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea that let ships reach Asia without sailing around Africa.
facts: In 2021, a giant container ship blocked it for six days, disrupting global supply chains.
Since it has no locks, ships pass through at sea level.

event-105.summary: The 1859 book in which Charles Darwin argued that living things have branched apart over immense spans of time.
facts: The first printing of 1,250 copies sold out immediately through bookseller orders alone.
The following year at Oxford, Huxley and Bishop Wilberforce clashed over evolution.

event-106.summary: In 1851, the first international exhibition, held in London in a vast hall of glass and iron filled with goods from around the world.
facts: Over five and a half months, 6 million people visited the hall, known as the Crystal Palace.
Continuing the tradition, the Eiffel Tower was built for a later exhibition in Paris.

event-107.summary: In 1903, two American bicycle-shop owners became the first to fly an airplane with an engine, staying aloft for 12 seconds.
facts: On December 17, they flew four times in a single day from sand dunes near Kitty Hawk.
They worked out on their own how to keep the plane balanced by twisting its wings.

event-108.summary: In 1949, the Communist Party, victorious in the civil war, proclaimed a new state in front of Tiananmen.
facts: October 1, the day Mao Zedong proclaimed its founding, is now China's National Day.
The defeated Nationalists retreated to Taiwan.

event-109.summary: In 1948, a Jewish state was established under a UN partition plan, and war broke out immediately.
facts: The day after it declared independence on May 14, neighboring Arab states invaded.
The plight of the Palestinians who fled their homes at this time remains unresolved today.

event-110.summary: The 1948 document in which the UN General Assembly stated that all people are born with the same rights.
facts: December 10, the day it was adopted, is now Human Rights Day.
With more than 570 translations, it is the most translated document in the world.

event-111.summary: For 20 years from 1955, a Cold War conflict in a country split into north and south, pitting the United States against communist forces.
facts: After the United States pulled out in 1973, Saigon fell in 1975 and the country was reunified.
South Korea also sent more than 320,000 troops starting in 1964.

event-112.summary: 1960, the year when seventeen countries on a single continent threw off colonial rule all at once.
facts: Fourteen of them were French colonies, and the number of independent countries on the continent rose from 9 to 26.
Nigeria, the Republic of the Congo, and Madagascar all gained independence that year.

event-113.summary: For ten years from 1966, a campaign to sweep away “the old” that wrecked schools, historic sites, and people alike.
facts: Mao Zedong launched it, and it ended only after his death in 1976.
Student Red Guards dragged out teachers and elders for public denunciation.

event-114.summary: In 1979, citizens overthrew the monarchy and turned the country into a state ruled by religious leaders.
facts: The Shah Pahlavi was driven out, and the exiled Khomeini returned to become Supreme Leader.
Oil prices soared, shaking the world economy.

event-115.summary: In 1986, a reactor exploded during a test at a power plant, sending radiation across the skies of Europe.
facts: The area within a 30-kilometer radius is still a restricted exclusion zone.
The nearby city of Pripyat was entirely evacuated the next day.

event-116.summary: In 1993, the nations of a continent that had fought two great wars agreed to open their borders and share a single currency.
facts: It came into being when a treaty signed in Maastricht, Netherlands, took effect.
It introduced the euro as a common currency in 1999, with notes and coins following in 2002.

event-117.summary: Born in 1969 as a research network funded by the US Department of Defense, this technology grew to link computers all over the world.
facts: The very first message was meant to be LOGIN, but the computer crashed after just two letters: LO.
In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee devised the World Wide Web at CERN in Geneva, Switzerland.

event-118.summary: In 2001, al-Qaeda hijacked four airliners and crashed them into the Twin Towers in New York City and the Pentagon.
facts: The attacks killed 2,977 people, more than the 2,403 who died at Pearl Harbor.
Two months later, the United States created the Transportation Security Administration, putting airport screening directly under federal control.

event-119.summary: In late 2019, a new infectious disease first reported in Wuhan, China, spread across the globe and brought borders and schools to a standstill.
facts: On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization declared a pandemic.
On December 8, 2020, a 90-year-old woman in the United Kingdom became the first person to receive a vaccine outside a clinical trial.
